title: Widen the admin dashboard's layout on large screens (especially the calendar)
tech: React + TypeScript frontend only -- CSS/layout change, no new dependency
keyConstraints: Investigated the root cause: frontend/src/styles/base.css's `.page` class is the single, globally shared page container -- used by every page in the app, admin AND customer AND login -- and it caps at `max-width: 640px` from its only breakpoint (`@media (min-width: 640px)`), with nothing beyond that for larger screens. So on any monitor wider than a small tablet, every admin view (List, Calendar, Availability, Services) renders inside a centered 640px column -- confirmed this is what makes AdminCalendar.tsx's grid (`.admin-calendar-grid`, which itself has no max-width and would happily fill more space) look cramped: the constraint is coming from its ancestor, not the calendar's own CSS. Ville confirmed the fix should be scoped to the admin dashboard ONLY -- the customer-facing booking flow (BookingWidget.tsx, ManageBooking.tsx) and both login pages (AdminLoginRequest.tsx, AdminLoginCallback.tsx) are simple linear forms that should stay at their current narrow/centered width even on large screens; do not widen the shared `.page` class itself, since that would affect those pages too. AdminDashboard.tsx's top-level return wraps its h1/logout button/view-mode switcher AND whichever sub-view is active (List content inline, or the conditionally-rendered <AdminCalendar>/<AdminAvailability>/<AdminServices>) in ONE outer `<div className="page">` (line ~145) -- so introducing a new class (or a modifier alongside `page`) on that single outer div would, in principle, widen all 4 admin views consistently in one place. HOWEVER: confirmed by reading AdminAvailability.tsx (line ~145, `<div className="admin-availability page">`) that it ALSO applies the `page` class to its own root div, nested inside AdminDashboard's outer `page` div -- meaning even if the outer wrapper is widened, AdminAvailability's content would still be re-clamped back down to 640px by its own redundant nested `.page` class, unless that's also addressed. AdminServices.tsx does not have this issue (`<div className="admin-services">`, no `page` class). AdminCalendar.tsx's own root (`<div className="admin-calendar">`) also has no competing width constraint. Architect should verify current computed widths in each of the 4 admin views before deciding the exact fix (e.g. a new `.page-admin` class replacing `.page` on AdminDashboard's outer div plus removing the redundant `page` class from AdminAvailability's inner div and relying on the outer wrapper alone; or some other approach) -- the goal is that all 4 admin views end up consistently wider on large screens, not just some of them by accident. Follow this codebase's established mobile-first CSS convention (base rules target narrow viewports, min-width media queries widen things back out -- see the comments at the top of base.css and AdminCalendar.css) rather than a desktop-first override. Pick a sensible upper bound for the widened admin container on very large screens (e.g. somewhere in the 1000-1400px range, informed by how AdminCalendar's grid actually looks at that width -- avoid stretching a 7-column month grid absurdly wide on an ultrawide monitor) -- Architect should decide and justify the exact value(s) and how many breakpoints are needed, rather than just removing the cap entirely. Existing narrow-viewport behavior (below 640px) must be completely unchanged.
description: The admin dashboard (List, Calendar, Availability, Services views) is currently capped at a 640px-wide centered column on every screen size, inherited from the same shared `.page` CSS class used by the customer booking flow and login pages. On larger monitors this leaves a lot of unused horizontal space, most noticeably in the calendar, whose own grid has no width constraint of its own and would use the extra room if its container allowed it. Widen the admin dashboard specifically (not the customer-facing or login pages) on large screens, so the calendar and other admin views make better use of bigger displays.
acceptanceCriteria: On large screens (above whatever breakpoint(s) the Architect defines), all 4 admin views (List, Calendar, Availability, Services) render noticeably wider than the current 640px cap -- verified in all four, not just the calendar
AdminAvailability.tsx's redundant nested `page` class (or equivalent re-clamping) is identified and resolved so it doesn't silently override the widened container

The customer-facing booking flow (BookingWidget.tsx, ManageBooking.tsx) and both admin login pages (AdminLoginRequest.tsx, AdminLoginCallback.tsx) are visually unchanged at every screen size -- confirmed by explicitly checking each of these pages before and after, not just assuming the admin-only change doesn't leak
Narrow/phone-width behavior (below 640px) is completely unchanged for every page in the app
The widened admin container has a sensible maximum width on very large/ultrawide screens -- not unbounded 100% width -- with the Architect's chosen value(s) justified
Existing mobile-first CSS convention followed (base rules narrow, min-width queries widen)

No regression to any existing test in AdminDashboard.test.tsx, AdminCalendar.test.tsx, AdminAvailability.test.tsx, AdminServices.test.tsx, BookingWidget.test.tsx, or ManageBooking.test.tsx -- run the full existing suite
npm test, npm run build, npm run lint, and tsc --noEmit all pass in frontend/ (backend unaffected, no backend files change)
relevantFilePaths: frontend/src/styles/base.css (.page class and its single existing breakpoint)

frontend/src/pages/AdminCalendar.tsx and AdminCalendar.css (the grid that should benefit from more width -- no changes expected here unless the Architect finds the grid itself needs adjustment at wide widths)
frontend/src/pages/AdminServices.tsx (read-only reference -- confirm no competing width constraint)

frontend/src/pages/BookingWidget.tsx, ManageBooking.tsx, AdminLoginRequest.tsx, AdminLoginCallback.tsx (read-only reference -- confirm these stay on the unmodified shared `.page` class and are visually unaffected)
securityConsiderations: None -- purely a CSS/layout change, no data handling, no new API calls, no new dependency.
